title: Why Do We Put Off Things We Actually Want to Do?
metaTitle: Why Do We Put Off Things We Actually Want to Do?
metaDescription: We don't only delay chores — we defer pleasures and meaningful goals too. Here is what research on savoring, saving, and present bias actually shows.
keyFinding: Deferring good things is common — partly because enjoyable experiences feel 'always available later' and 'someday' feels infinite — and naming that pattern is part of what helps people actually do them.
honestAnswer: Because the things we want to do rarely feel urgent, and 'later' feels safe. We tend to assume meaningful and enjoyable experiences will always be available, so there is no deadline forcing them — and without a deadline, the easy default usually wins. The result is that we put off not just chores but the very things we say we most want.

This is a common pattern, not a personal failing. Several research threads point to it: we treat pleasures as endlessly available and then never get to them; we save special things for an occasion that never quite arrives; the easy option tends to win in the moment; and anticipating something can feel safer than the riskier act of doing it. Naming the pattern is part of what helps, because 'someday' only keeps its grip while it stays unexamined.
whatDataShows: Research on savoring (Jordi Quoidbach and colleagues, among others) explores how people derive enjoyment from positive experiences — and a recurring theme is that we often fail to capitalise on pleasures that are readily available. When something good feels constantly accessible, it loses its sense of occasion, and we defer it indefinitely rather than actually engaging with it.

A related line of work on 'saving for a special occasion' finds that people frequently hoard nice things — a good bottle, a special outfit, a gift — waiting for a moment worthy of them, and that the awaited occasion often never comes, so the item goes unused or wasted. The instinct to preserve the special thing can quietly prevent us from ever enjoying it.

On the mechanics, present bias — our tendency to overweight the immediate over the future — favours the easy default now over the more effortful good thing. There is also an 'activation energy' cost: the meaningful activity usually requires more setup than the passive alternative. And anticipation research suggests that looking forward to something can itself be pleasurable, and sometimes feel safer than the act, which can subtly reinforce keeping the experience in the future rather than the present.
whyItFeelsDifferent: It feels different from ordinary procrastination because there is no obvious cost. Putting off a chore has a looming consequence; putting off a pleasure or a meaningful goal has none that announces itself, so it never triggers the urgency that would push us to act. The thing we want simply stays parked in 'later.'

'Someday' also feels infinite. As long as the experience seems endlessly available, there is no reason to choose it today over anything else — and so we never do. The very abundance of opportunity removes the scarcity that makes us act, which is why readily available pleasures are so easy to keep deferring.

And anticipation can feel better, or at least safer, than the thing itself. Looking forward to a trip, a project, or a long-wanted experience carries no risk of disappointment, awkwardness, or effort. Keeping it in the future preserves the pleasant anticipation and avoids the gamble of the real attempt, which makes deferral quietly tempting.
whatResearchSaysToDo: The most consistent counter to deferral is to remove the indefiniteness — to give the good thing a time, not just an intention. Because 'someday' has no deadline, the experiences that get done are usually the ones that get scheduled. Putting a meaningful or enjoyable activity on the calendar converts an open-ended wish into a concrete plan.

Treating availability as scarcer than it feels helps too. The savoring research suggests that we under-enjoy what feels constantly accessible, so deliberately framing a pleasure as a now-or-not opportunity — using the nice thing, taking the experience while you can — counteracts the 'always available later' trap that leads to saving things into oblivion.

Lowering the activation energy makes the meaningful option more likely to win against the easy default. Reducing the setup required, removing small frictions, and making the good thing the path of least resistance all help present bias work for you rather than against you. And simply naming the pattern — recognising that you keep deferring something you genuinely want — is itself a documented prompt to act.
whatDoesNotHelp: Waiting for the perfect occasion does not help — it is one of the main ways good things go unused. The 'special occasion' that justifies the saved bottle, the unworn outfit, or the long-planned trip often never arrives, so hoarding the experience for a worthier moment tends to mean never having it at all.

Relying on future motivation rarely works, because present bias predictably favours the easy default again tomorrow. Telling yourself you will do the meaningful thing when you feel more like it usually just relocates the deferral; the conditions you are waiting for are no more likely to appear later than now.

And over-investing in anticipation as a substitute for action can quietly prevent the experience. Endlessly looking forward to something, while comfortable and even pleasurable, can become a way of keeping it safely in the future rather than ever risking the real, imperfect, present-tense version of it.
realNumbersInContext: This topic is better captured by patterns than by precise statistics, and any hard number here should be treated cautiously. The well-supported findings are qualitative: people under-enjoy readily available pleasures (savoring research), commonly save special things for occasions that never come, and are pulled toward easy defaults by present bias and activation-energy costs.

The honest takeaway is directional rather than numerical. Deferring things we genuinely want is common and has identifiable causes — 'always available later,' the wait for a special occasion, the pull of the easy default, and the safety of anticipation. Because the causes are nameable, the pattern is workable: scheduling the good thing, treating it as scarce, and lowering the effort to start are the steps the research most supports.

keyTakeaways: We defer not just chores but the very things we most want to do, because they rarely feel urgent.
Pleasures that feel 'always available later' lose their sense of occasion and get put off indefinitely.
Saving special things for a worthy moment often means the moment never comes and the thing goes unused.
Anticipation can feel safer than the act, so keeping an experience in the future quietly becomes the default.
Naming the pattern and giving the good thing a time — not just an intention — is what most helps.

examples.label: Illustrative
examples.title: The bottle saved for a special occasion
examples.body: A good bottle sits in the cupboard for years, waiting for a moment worthy of it. The instinct to preserve the special thing feels responsible, but the worthy occasion never quite arrives — and eventually the bottle is past its best, or forgotten. Hoarding the experience for a better moment turned out to mean never having it at all.

examples.label: Illustrative
examples.title: The trip that stays in 'someday'
examples.body: The long-wanted trip keeps getting deferred, not because anything blocks it but because it never feels urgent — there's always next year. And looking forward to it carries no risk of effort or disappointment, while actually booking it does. Anticipation is comfortable enough that it can quietly substitute for the trip itself. Giving it a date on the calendar is what converts the wish into a plan.

faqs.question: Why do I put off things I actually want to do?
faqs.answer: Largely because they don't feel urgent. We assume enjoyable and meaningful experiences will always be available, so 'later' feels safe and the easy default wins in the moment. Without a deadline, present bias and the effort of getting started keep pushing the good thing into a 'someday' that never arrives.

faqs.question: Why do I save nice things for a special occasion and never use them?
faqs.answer: Research on 'saving for a special occasion' finds people commonly hoard nice things waiting for a moment worthy of them — and that the awaited occasion often never comes, so the item goes unused. The instinct to preserve the special thing can quietly prevent you from ever enjoying it.

faqs.question: Is this just procrastination?
faqs.answer: It overlaps but feels different, because deferring a pleasure has no looming consequence the way deferring a chore does. There's nothing to trigger urgency, so the thing you want simply stays in 'later.' The savoring research adds that we tend to under-enjoy whatever feels constantly available.

faqs.question: Why does looking forward to something feel better than doing it?
faqs.answer: Anticipation carries no risk of effort, awkwardness, or disappointment, while the real act does. Keeping an experience in the future preserves the pleasant anticipation and avoids the gamble of the real attempt, which can subtly reinforce deferring it rather than doing it.

faqs.question: How do I actually stop deferring the things I want?
faqs.answer: Give the good thing a time rather than an intention — scheduling beats 'someday.' Treat the pleasure as scarcer than it feels (use the nice thing now), lower the effort needed to start, and name the pattern when you notice it. Recognising the deferral is itself a documented prompt to act.
